fullText:
Super interesting work from Microsoft and colleagues.

They take a closer look at the exciting research area of weight-space programming.

They had Claude Opus 5.5 write transformer weights directly in code, with no gradient training.

The smallest models that solved the algorithmic tasks had a median of 166 parameters.

The method is called interpretable weight-space programming. An agent proposes a computation, writes it as explicit weights and features, tests it, and revises it for 30 to 50 rounds. A person can read the result line by line.

All 26 runs on algorithmic tasks reached 100% accuracy on held-out data, often by writing a known algorithm into the weights.

They find that the model matters. Sonnet 5.5 needed a median of 41,600 parameters, and Haiku 5.5 needed 100,000.

Language tasks were harder. Those models stayed near 190,000 parameters and lost accuracy against learned baselines.

They then used the same loop on brain data. In the visual cortex, it predicted responses better than existing interpretable models. In language fMRI, it found a confound in the dataset.

https://t.co/JKYdkdLqwV

fullText:
in a $40 trillion market with 3 and perhaps 4 players, that SpaceX can provide the key supply input at the margin at scale (and can alternatively use that supply to directly compete in the market), results in an equilibrium where the marginal price per compute can get to obscene levels.

the simple logic is that openAI and anthropic have non SpaceX future compute reserved, and so enter into a race condition to train and serve a somewhat sticky market so that they can maximize internal margins on the reserved compute once the market has saturated; even knowing that SpaceX will eventually pull compute in-house to occupy the majority of the market this is optimal strategy.

Even knowing that they won't be able to occupy the majority of the market due to spaceX's compute dominance, they overpay in the near term to maximize their long-term profitability serving a meaningful minority of the market with the compute they do have secured.

fullText:
If you have a fear of math, it is not organic. It was planted in your brain by another person who was afraid of math. Get over it. Learn the beauty, magic, and mystery of mathematics. Thank me later!

True story:  Among the various undergraduate and graduate courses that I taught was an introductory computational & data sciences course at the University (GMU). Many of my students in the first day of class expressed strongly their fear of math and hoped that the course was only low-level math. I told them not to worry—I would teach them whatever math they needed to know. So, I taught them calculus (integral and differential) but I didn’t tell them it was calculus until after their first quiz and homework assignments involving calculus. When I finally told them that they had just learned calculus, they were stunned. Some had tears in their eyes. Some thanked me profusely saying it was best course they ever had and they wanted to learn more math. In fact, the one young man who was most adamant against math on the first day of class, by the end of the semester, was the most profoundly changed and grateful student that I ever taught. I still remember his handshake after the final exam and the excitement in his voice looking forward to taking more math courses—to make up for all that he missed previously due to misinformed fear. (This is a true story, not AI slop.)

Mathematics, Magic and Mystery: https://t.co/ZHYc9peUCY

user.name: Gary Marcus
user.description: OG GenAI Skeptic; spoke at US Senate. Warned about hallucinations in 2001. Advocating world models & neurosymbolic AI ever since. Author, Marcus on AI & 6 books

fullText:
The 🗝️ fact:  You can’t understand contemporary AI unless you can appreciate the difference between a model (that is part of a system) and a system as a whole.

If a system as a whole includes both neural networks and symbols, it is by definition neurosymbolic.

To think otherwise is like thinking that an engine IS a car, rather than a component of a car. You can’t make a car out of engines alone. and you can’t (in most cases) make robust, reliable AI systems out of neural networks alone.

Instead, in many domains you get better results by  *integrating* both neural networks and symbols. (Math, where e.g., Lean checks and sometimes rejects the work of LLMs is a good example of this; so is Claude Code).

That was literally the point of my 2001 book The Algebraic Mind and has been a central point throughout my career.

For a long time, people like @GeoffreyHinton argued otherwise, suggesting that all we needed were neural networks by themselves, and that symbols were an archaic waste of time. Hinton likened symbols to “aether”, as if they were complete scientific mistake.

He was wrong. Systems like Claude Code depend heavily on combining neural networks with things like rules, code interpreters, functions, conditionals and loops - all symbolic constructs drawn from classical AI. Math systems use automated theorem provers, which flow directly from Newell and Simon’s symbolic work in the 1950s.

Symbols weren’t a mistake; they were vital, just as neural networks are.  Scaling helped, but by itself it wasn’t enough; symbolic tools and code interpreters and harnesses are now a central part of most working systems.

Neurosymbolic AI has won, overwhelmingly; the pure neural networks that the dogmatists like Hinton used to argue for have been almost entirely displaced by neurosymbolic hybrids.

As @fchollet has also noted, to pretend otherwise is just silly.
